Fast, Cheap, and Fair? Evaluating Decision Models

Abstract

Industries are increasingly adopting AI-driven systems to automate a wide range of tasks, including high-stakes decisions in human resources, such as candidate screening and recruitment. This makes evaluating their fairness essential, particularly when decisions directly affect individuals’ opportunities. Accordingly, the EU AI Act classifies recruitment AI systems as high-risk, imposing strict requirements on their deployment. In this context, compact “System 1” decision models offer a fast and cost-efficient alternative to general-purpose LLMs, yet their fairness remains largely unexplored. This article presents the first systematic bias and fairness audit of JEV, a typed-decision model targeting recruitment applications. The study evaluates how explicit demographic attributes and implicit candidate cues influence screening scores, rankings, and shortlisting outcomes. These effects are compared against a noise floor derived from name substitutions and typographical variations. The evaluation also examines output validity, latency, and cost. Counterfactual CV datasets and evaluation code are released for reproducibility.

1 Introduction

AI systems are increasingly used to automate industrial workflows, from customer-service assistance to Human Resources (HR) tasks such as candidate screening and shortlisting (Ul Haq et al., 2024; Yao et al., 2025). These applications often rely on Generative Models, particularly LLMs, which produce textual outputs token by token, even when the task requires only a score or a decision. At industrial scale, repeated model calls make latency and cost critical constraints (Chen et al., 2024). An emerging alternative is offered by Decision Models, which directly map inputs to labels or probabilities without generating text. This distinction can be understood through dual-process theory, which differentiates fast, automatic “System 1” thinking from slower, deliberative “System 2” reasoning (Kahneman, 2011; Booch et al., 2021). By analogy, Decision Models act as “System 1”, offering faster and less expensive predictions, whereas Generative Models resemble “System 2”.

However, efficiency alone does not guarantee fairness, particularly in high-stakes applications such as recruitment, where automated decisions directly affect individuals’ opportunities. The EU AI Act classifies AI systems used in recruitment as high-risk (European Parliament and Council of the European Union, 2024), while New York City’s Local Law 144 requires bias audits of automated employment decision tools (Council of the City of New York, 2021). Numerous studies have investigated demographic biases in LLM-based recruitment, demonstrating that candidate evaluations can change when only names or identity-related attributes are modified (An et al., 2024; Nghiem et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024; An et al., 2025). Similar concerns have been reported for embedding-based retrieval systems (Wilson and Caliskan, 2024; Seshadri et al., 2025). In contrast, existing evaluations of Decision Models have primarily examined accuracy, calibration, and robustness (Deußer et al., 2026; Tang and Zheng, 2026), with preliminary evidence of demographic effects in pricing applications (Imperatrice et al., 2026). Their fairness in high-stakes recruitment, particularly in comparison with Generative Models, remains unexplored.

To address this gap, this article presents a comparative evaluation of two Decision Models, JEV TypeSafe AI (2026) and Laya (Convai Innovations, 2026), and two Generative Models, specifically GPT-6 Luna and GPT-6.1 Sol. Using counterfactual CVs, the study examines how explicit and implicit demographic signals related to gender, ethnicity, and origin affect candidate scores, rankings, and top-5 shortlists. These effects are compared against run-to-run variability under identical inputs to distinguish systematic bias from model instability. The evaluation also considers decision validity, latency, and cost, and extends the fairness analysis to the decision-making scenarios of Tamkin et al. (2023).

The main contributions of this article are summarized as follows: (i) Consistency Analysis: an examination of run-to-run variability in both model classes, showing how the instability of Generative Models can mask or exceed demographic bias and lead to misleading conclusions when fairness is assessed using a single run (ii) Bias Analysis: a counterfactual audit of Decision and Generative Models in candidate screening, examining the effects of explicit and implicit demographic signals on candidate scores, rankings, and shortlisting decisions (iii) Validity Assessment: an evaluation of screening decisions against ground-truth labels to assess how closely both model classes align with the ground truth (iv) Efficiency Comparison: an assessment of inference latency and cost for both model classes using identical inputs.

2 Related Work

Bias in Automated Screening

Counterfactual auditing evaluates fairness by modifying a single demographic attribute while keeping the remaining candidate information unchanged. Originating from field experiments that revealed racial and gender disparities in hiring (Bertrand and Mullainathan, 2004; Kline et al., 2022), this approach has become widely used to audit automated screening systems (Gaebler et al., 2024). Studies have identified demographic biases in traditional classifiers and embedding-based retrievers (De-Arteaga et al., 2019; Wilson and Caliskan, 2024), as well as in LLM-based recruitment systems, where outcomes vary with candidate names, prompt wording, and occupation (An et al., 2024; Nghiem et al., 2024; Armstrong et al., 2024; An et al., 2025). More recent findings regarding post-2024 models suggest that bias patterns have shifted across model generations, sometimes favoring previously disadvantaged groups (Gao et al., 2026b; Rozado, 2026). Discrimination can also arise through indirect signals, including dialect, university prestige, disability, and graduation year (Hofmann et al., 2024; Iso et al., 2025; Glazko et al., 2024; Bone et al., 2026). However, demographic changes are not the only source of variation: name substitutions and formatting edits can produce comparable changes in candidate rankings (Seshadri et al., 2025), highlighting the importance of distinguishing bias from instability. Existing evaluations also examine ranking disparities (Wang et al., 2024), discriminatory decision probabilities (Tamkin et al., 2023), and screening validity (Castleman et al., 2026).

Decision Models

Unlike Generative Models, Decision Models directly return probability distributions over predefined options. Recent systems include JEV (TypeSafe AI, 2026) and the open alternative Laya (Convai Innovations, 2026). On public benchmarks, JEV performs strongly, outperforming two open-weight LLMs on most of 37 datasets at very low cost (Deußer et al., 2026). It still trails stronger hosted LLMs on social-science annotation and legal inference (Ibrahim and Zaki, 2026; Zhang et al., 2026), and its errors largely coincide with those of LLM judges (Rao and Callison-Burch, 2026). However, a review of the first studies finds its clearest advantages in latency and cost rather than accuracy (Tang and Zheng, 2026). Nevertheless, reliability remains a concern, as predictions can vary across repeated requests, option orderings, and formatting changes (Zhang et al., 2026; Du et al., 2026).

Bias in Decision Models

Despite their efficiency, Decision Models exhibit sensitivity to option names, ordinal rating scales, and underrepresented input groups (Sun et al., 2026; Gao et al., 2026a; Liu, 2026). Although JEV has been used to identify social biases in other models (Guo et al., 2026), direct investigations of its own demographic fairness remain limited. In a car-pricing scenario, Imperatrice et al. (2026) identified small demographic differences without comparing them against Generative Models.

Research Gap and Contribution

Building on prior research, the present study examines demographic fairness in recruitment screening through a comparative evaluation of Decision and Generative Models. The analysis considers bias, screening validity, and computational efficiency while accounting for run-to-run variability to distinguish systematic demographic disparities from model instability.

3 Methodology

3.1 Problem Formulation

Each screening instance consists of a job description Jj∈𝒥J_{j}\in\mathcal{J} and a pool Pj={X1,…,Xnj}⊂𝒳P_{j}=\{X_{1},\dots,X_{n_{j}}\}\subset\mathcal{X} of njn_{j} CVs belonging to the same occupation. For each job-CV pair (Jj,Xi)(J_{j},X_{i}), a model mm independently assigns a match score sj​im∈[0,100]s^{m}_{ji}\in[0,100] that indicates how well the CV fits the job description, with higher values indicating a better fit. This score is mapped to a predicted label through λ:[0,100]→ℒ\lambda:[0,100]\rightarrow\mathcal{L}, where ℒ={Fit,NotFit}\mathcal{L}=\{\textsc{Fit},\textsc{NotFit}\}. Within each pool PjP_{j}, CVs are ranked in descending order of their match scores, with rj​imr^{m}_{ji} denoting the rank of CV XiX_{i}. Finally, Im={(j,i):Xi∈Pj}I^{m}=\{(j,i):X_{i}\in P_{j}\} denotes the set of all job-CV pairs evaluated by model mm, while Im,k={(j,i)∈Im:rj​im≤k}I^{m,k}=\{(j,i)\in I^{m}:r^{m}_{ji}\leq k\} denotes the subset corresponding to the top kk ranked CVs in each pool. For readability, the model superscript mm is omitted when clear from context.

3.2 Datasets

The evaluation uses two publicly available datasets: (i) hiring-fairness, a subset of the Kaggle Resume dataset (Bhawal, 2021) used by Seshadri et al. (2025), containing CVs across 11 occupations, paired with job descriptions and organized into candidate pools (ii) JD-Fit, the resume-job-description-fit dataset,11 1 https://huggingface.co/datasets/cnamuangtoun/resume-job-description-fit with gold labels binarized into Fit (Good or Potential Fit) and NotFit. The first dataset lacks gold labels and is therefore used for bias analysis, while JD-Fit provides them and is used to assess predictive validity. Additional bias analysis on JD-Fit is omitted due to computational costs. More information on dataset statistics is reported in Appendix A.

3.3 Counterfactual Design

Following correspondence audits (Bertrand and Mullainathan, 2004) and their adaptation to language models (Wilson and Caliskan, 2024; Seshadri et al., 2025), this study constructs a counterfactual CV Xi(a,g,σ)X_{i}^{(a,g,\sigma)} by introducing a single demographic signal for group gg in attribute aa, e.g., group Black for the Ethnicity attribute. The signal is introduced either explicitly, by adding a demographic attribute at the top of the CV, or implicitly, through the candidate’s name, with σ∈{explicit,implicit}\sigma\in\{\textsc{explicit},\textsc{implicit}\}. All other CV information remains unchanged, and each counterfactual replaces the original CV XiX_{i} in its pool and is re-scored, while the scores of all other candidates are held fixed. The resulting score and rank are denoted by sj​i(a,g,σ)s_{ji}^{(a,g,\sigma)} and rj​i(a,g,σ)r_{ji}^{(a,g,\sigma)}, respectively.

To account for model instability, a null counterfactual is obtained by evaluating the original CVs in tt independent runs, yielding sj​i(t)s^{(t)}_{ji} and rj​i(t)r^{(t)}_{ji}. The variation across these runs establishes a baseline against which demographic effects are assessed.

3.4 Models and Prompts

Four models are evaluated: two Decision Models, JEV and Laya, and two Generative Models, GPT-6 Luna and GPT-6.1 Sol. All models receive identical inputs and evaluate candidates using the same fixed rubric, which comprises seven criteria for: (i) required skills (ii) experience (iii) seniority (iv) domain (v) preferred skills (vi) education (vii) evidence . Specific details about the rubric scores, prompt construction and implementation details are reported in Appendices B, C, and D, respectively.

Both Decision Models and Generative Models assess candidates against the seven rubric criteria but produce different outputs. For each criterion, Decision Models return probability distributions over predefined answer levels, while Generative Models select a single level. These outputs are normalized and combined into a weighted match score from 0 to 100, with two eligibility conditions controlling the inclusion of preferred skills and education. The scoring procedure is identical across models, so differences reflect their rubric evaluations.

3.5 Metrics

Consistency Analysis

On unchanged CVs, run-to-run consistency is assessed across 77 independent runs using ICC (Shrout and Fleiss, 1979) to measure score agreement, the per-CV standard deviation of scores (σ\sigmaScore) and ranks (σ\sigmaRank), and the proportion of labels λ⁡(s)\lambda(s) that differ from each CV’s most frequent label.

Shortlist stability is measured with disagreement score (Disag​@​5\mathrm{Disag@5}) on the unchanged CVs. Each CV’s scores are averaged over the 7 runs, and the five CVs with the highest mean score in each pool form the reference shortlist I¯5\bar{I}^{5}. Each run is then compared with this reference by counting how many reference CVs fall outside that run’s top 5:

Disag​@​5=1007​∑t=171|I¯5|​∑(j,i)∈I¯5(1−hj​it),\displaystyle\mathrm{Disag@5}=\frac{100}{7}\sum_{t=1}^{7}\frac{1}{|\bar{I}^{5}|}\sum_{(j,i)\in\bar{I}^{5}}\big(1-h^{t}_{ji}\big), (1)

where hj​it=1h^{t}_{ji}=1 if CV XiX_{i} is in the top 5 of pool PjP_{j} in run tt and 00 otherwise; CVs tied at rank 5 share the remaining places (e.g., hj​it=0.5h^{t}_{ji}=0.5 for two CVs tied for the last place).

Bias Analysis

On hiring-fairness, three metrics quantify demographic effects on screening outcomes (Seshadri et al., 2025):

Δ​Score\displaystyle\Delta\mathrm{Score} =1|I|​∑(j,i)∈I[sj​i(a,g,σ)−sj​i(a,gref,σ)],\displaystyle=\frac{1}{|I|}\sum_{(j,i)\in I}\left[s_{ji}^{(a,g,\sigma)}-s_{ji}^{(a,g^{\mathrm{ref}},\sigma)}\right], (2)
Δ​Rank\displaystyle\Delta\mathrm{Rank} =1|I|​∑(j,i)∈I[rj​i−rj​i(a,g,σ)],\displaystyle=\frac{1}{|I|}\sum_{(j,i)\in I}\left[r_{ji}-r_{ji}^{(a,g,\sigma)}\right], (3)
Excl​@​5\displaystyle\mathrm{Excl@5} =100|I5|∑(j,i)∈I5𝕀[rj​i(a,g,σ)>5],\displaystyle=\frac{100}{|I^{5}|}\sum_{(j,i)\in I^{5}}\mathbb{I}\left[r_{ji}^{(a,g,\sigma)}>5\right], (4)

where grefg^{\mathrm{ref}} denotes the reference group and 𝕀\mathbb{I} the indicator function. The score displacement (Δ​Score\Delta\mathrm{Score}) quantifies changes in screening scores induced by explicit or implicit demographic cues, relative to a reference group and holding CV qualifications constant (level bias) (Wang et al., 2024). The rank displacement (Δ​Rank\Delta\mathrm{Rank}) captures ranking changes relative to the original CVs, while the exclusion rate (Excl​@​5\mathrm{Excl@5}) measures the percentage of originally top-55 candidates excluded after demographic modification. Across metrics, values closer to zero indicate smaller observed demographic effects.

Validity Assessment and Efficiency Comparison

On JD-Fit, validity is assessed using ROC AUC (Hanley and McNeil, 1982; Fawcett, 2006), its difference Δ​AUC=AUCm−AUCJEV\Delta\mathrm{AUC}=\mathrm{AUC}_{m}-\mathrm{AUC}_{\textnormal{JEV}} between the evaluated model mm and the JEV reference evaluator, Balanced Accuracy (Brodersen et al., 2010) and Macro-F1 at the model-specific thresholds calibrated on 50 training job descriptions and evaluated on 1759 test, and Precision@5 (Manning et al., 2008) which measures the share of Fit CVs among the five top-ranked CVs of each job description, averaged over job descriptions. The average proportion of Fit CVs per job description is 0.570.57, establishing a random ranking baseline. Efficiency is assessed using median and 95th-percentile per-call Latency in seconds, and estimated Cost per 1000 calls based on prices reported in Appendix D.

Statistical Significance

Statistical significance is assessed using 2000 paired bootstrap resamples, with CVs, scenarios, or job descriptions as sampling units. For bias analyses, two-sided pp-values are adjusted using the Benjamini–Hochberg correction (∗: q<0.05q<0.05). For validity, ∗ marks 95%95\% confidence intervals excluding chance or zero for Δ​AUC\Delta\mathrm{AUC}. More details are reported in Appendix E.

4 Results and Analysis

4.1 Consistency Analysis

Table 1 shows that JEV is nearly deterministic, while the Generative Models are not. Across 7 runs on the 572 CVs in hiring-fairness, JEV’s scores agree almost perfectly: scores and rankings remain highly stable, with very few changes in labels or shortlist membership. This aligns with the low run-to-run variation reported by Tang and Zheng (2026) and Du et al. (2026). The Generative Models are less consistent, with GPT-6 Luna’s scores varying up to eight times more than JEV’s. Shortlist changes reach 18% for GPT-6.1 Sol and 30% for GPT-6 Luna, partly due to more frequent ties at the cut-off caused by their coarser scoring scales (more details are reported in Appendix F). This instability persists under the audited configuration, as reasoning-enabled models accept only the default sampling temperature,22 2 The API supports custom temperature and top_p values only when reasoning effort is none. producing different decisions despite identical inputs and prompts. This aligns with previous findings that stable aggregate scores may mask variability in individual decisions (Zhang et al., 2026). Laya, instead, is fully deterministic. In hiring, such instability raises fairness concerns, as shortlisting outcomes depend partly on the run, making repeated evaluations necessary to distinguish bias from noise.

4.2 Bias Analysis

Table 2 reports the bias results on hiring-fairness, showing that JEV follow the direction of recent LLMs, slightly favoring Female over Male CVs and Black or Hispanic over White CVs. This aligns with findings for post 2024 LLMs, which reverse earlier patterns by favoring women and, in some studies, Black candidates (An et al., 2025; Gao et al., 2026b; Rozado, 2026). Despite 11 out of 16 Δ\DeltaScore effects and 13 out of 22 Δ\DeltaRank effects being statistically significant, JEV’s biases remain small: Δ\DeltaScore peaks at 0.370.37 points, Δ\DeltaRank stays below 0.40.4 positions in pools of 41–65 CVs, and Excl​@​5\mathrm{Excl@5} reaches 8.2%8.2\% against a 2.9%2.9\% in run-to-run variation, equivalent to about 3 additional CVs across pools. Such small effects are visible also thanks to JEV’s high stability across runs.

Another interesting finding is that names, rather than explicitly stated attributes, drive JEV’s remaining effects. Explicitly stating Asian ethnicity has negligible effect, while Asian names lower scores by 0.110.11 points relative to White names. Male, White, and Asian names also lower ranks by 0.370.37, 0.240.24, and 0.380.38 positions, respectively, exceeding the effects of explicit attributes. This aligns with Seshadri et al. (2025), who show that names influence rankings beyond their demographic signals. Since Δ​Rank\Delta\mathrm{Rank} and Excl​@​5\mathrm{Excl@5} are calculated relative to the unmodified CV, their estimates capture both the effect of adding a name and any group-specific effect. Differences between groups should therefore be assessed against the reference group’s values.

Neither GPT-6 Luna nor GPT-6.1 Sol shows statistically significant Δ\DeltaScore or Δ\DeltaRank effects, but this does not imply absence of bias. GPT-6 Luna’s estimates are comparable to JEV’s, yet its run-to-run variation is eight times larger as shown in Table 1. Excl​@​5\mathrm{Excl@5} ranges from 24.524.5–50.050.0% for GPT-6 Luna and 3.73.7–14.8%14.8\% for GPT-6.1 Sol, near their respective run-to-run variations of 29.6%29.6\% and 18.3%18.3\%. Therefore, demographic modifications produce shortlist changes comparable to ordinary reruns, or even smaller changes for GPT-6.1 Sol, suggesting that model instability can obscure demographic bias and highlighting the importance of assessing bias relative to run-to-run variation.

Despite producing identical outputs across repeated runs, as shown in Table 1, Laya is sensitive to small CV modifications, which shift nearly all candidates, including reference groups, down one or two ranks (Δ\DeltaRank) and exclude 11.811.8–23.5%23.5\% of shortlisted candidates.

4.3 Validity Assessment

Table 3 reports the results on the JD-Fit dataset, demonstrating that JEV’s shortlist quality is comparable to that of the Generative Models, with JEV, GPT-6 Luna, and GPT-6.1 Sol all distinguishing Fit from NotFit pairs well above chance. Neither Generative Model significantly outperforms JEV, with AUC differences of just 0.0150.015 for GPT-6 Luna and 0.0050.005 for GPT-6.1 Sol, making their ranking performance practically indistinguishable. At calibrated thresholds, GPT-6 Luna achieves about two points higher Balanced Accuracy and Macro-F1, mainly due to fewer false positives (Figure 1, 308 vs. 336), while the more expensive GPT-6.1 Sol offers no significant improvement over JEV. In contrast, Laya shows limited Validity, with an AUC of 0.5200.520 not significantly above chance and 0.1120.112 below JEV’s, and Precision@5 of 0.5990.599 close to random chance. Thus, despite producing identical outputs across runs, Laya exhibits screening bias and limited predictive validity, demonstrating that determinism alone does not ensure reliability.

Figure 1 shows the JD-Fit test predictions of each model at its tuned threshold (902 Fit and 857 NotFit pairs). JEV and GPT-6 Luna make similar trade-offs: both recognize about 57–58% of Fit pairs, and GPT-6 Luna’s higher balanced accuracy comes mainly from fewer false positives (308 vs. 336 NotFit pairs predicted as Fit). GPT-6.1 Sol reaches the same balanced accuracy as JEV with a more conservative threshold: it predicts Fit for only 37%37\% of pairs, which gives the highest share of correct NotFit predictions (72%72\%) but misses more than half of the Fit pairs (54%). In screening, such misses correspond to qualified candidates who are rejected. Laya predicts Fit for 57%57\% of pairs and identifies only 45%45\% of NotFit pairs correctly, in line with its near-chance AUC.

4.4 Efficiency Comparison

On JD-Fit, JEV is 24–33×\times faster than Generative Models, screening 1000 CVs in about 5 minutes versus 2–3 hours, as shown in Figure 2. Experimental costs were $4.26\$4.26 for JEV, $23.23\$23.23 for GPT-6 Luna, and $290.87\$290.87 for GPT-6.1 Sol, making JEV 5–68×\times cheaper, as reported in Table 4. This reflects JEV’s input-only billing, which avoids the output and reasoning costs of Generative Models. Combined with the comparable shortlist quality reported in Section 4.3, JEV achieves 33–4%4\% of their latency and 1.51.5–18%18\% of their cost.

5 Conclusion

This study presents a fairness audit of JEV in recruitment screening, comparing it with frontier Generative Models and an open-source Decision Model across bias, validity, efficiency, and consistency. JEV delivers a stronger performance-efficiency trade-off than frontier Generative Models, achieving similar predictive Validity with greater run-to-run consistency, up to 33×\times faster inference, and 67×\times lower costs. However, small but measurable demographic biases persist, particularly through implicit cues such as names. These findings support JEV for large-scale recruitment screening, subject to fairness audits and human oversight. Future work should explore other languages, agentic pipelines, and bias mitigation for Decision Models.

Limitations

The bias evaluation covers one dataset: hiring-fairness contains 572 English CVs and 11 job descriptions across 11 occupations. Findings may therefore not generalize to other occupations, languages, or decision tasks. Moreover, the evaluation covers gender, ethnicity, and origin in CV screening, excluding attributes such as disability, religion, socioeconomic status, and intersectional groups.

Beyond dataset coverage, the counterfactual approach simplifies how demographics are conveyed in real CVs. Attributes are introduced through a single line containing an explicit statement or a name, whereas real CVs may signal demographics indirectly through schools, affiliations, or career gaps. Names can also convey nationality, social class, or age beyond the intended attribute. Furthermore, the LLM-generated name lists follow US and UK conventions, include only two names per group, and treat gender as binary in CV screening. Implicit effects may therefore depend partly on the names selected.

Given these limitations, the experiments measure model responses to controlled English-language CVs modifications rather than disparate impacts on actual applicant pools or downstream hiring outcomes. Consequently, the results do not certify any model as fair for hiring. Deployments should instead conduct domain-specific audits using real applicant data, repeat evaluations after model updates, and maintain human oversight of automated decisions.

Appendix A Datasets

Two datasets are used in this study: hiring-fairness for counterfactual bias and consistency in CV screening and JD-Fit for validity.

A.1 hiring-fairness

hiring-fairness is built from the Kaggle part of the hiring-fairness benchmark of Seshadri et al. (2025), which pairs LinkedIn job descriptions from 11 occupations with real CVs from the Kaggle Resume Dataset (Bhawal, 2021); the CVs contain no candidate names. One job description is drawn per occupation with a fixed seed and scored against all CVs of that occupation, resulting in 11 job descriptions and 572 CVs (41–65 per pool), which are visible in Table 5. Following correspondence audits (Bertrand and Mullainathan, 2004) and their adaptation to language models (An et al., 2024; Wilson and Caliskan, 2024), each counterfactual inserts exactly one line at the top of the CV and leaves the rest unchanged: an attribute line for explicit signals, or only a name for implicit signals (Table 6). For implicit ethnicity and origin, each CV receives names of one gender in all its versions, so gender does not confound group differences. Names were generated by GPT-6 Luna with the prompts in Figure 3. For consistency, the unchanged CVs are scored in 7 independent runs.

A.2 JD-Fit

JD-Fit is the resume-job-description-fit dataset on Hugging Face,33 3 https://huggingface.co/datasets/cnamuangtoun/resume-job-description-fit with (job description, CV) pairs labeled Good, Potential or No Fit and split into train and test by job description. Good and Potential Fit are mapped to Fit and No Fit to NotFit, and conflicting and duplicate pairs are removed. Whole job descriptions are sampled so that each CV pool stays complete: the test set contains all 1759 test pairs from 71 job descriptions (902 Fit, 857 NotFit), and a tuning set of 1605 pairs from 50 training job descriptions with at least 10 CVs and both labels is used only to choose each model’s threshold. The source had replaced candidate names with a female placeholder name (e.g., “Jessica Claire”), which would add the same gender signal to every CV; rule-based edits remove the placeholder and contact details, restore words garbled by the replacement, replace pronouns referring to the candidate with they, and remove explicit gender, age and citizenship statements. Each pair is scored once per model with the rubric and prompt described in Appendix B and Appendix C.

Appendix B Rubrics

For each pair (Jj,Xi)(J_{j},X_{i}) on hiring-fairness and JD-Fit, every model answers the same rubric reported in Table 7: a set QQ of seven scored questions on described scales and two yes/no gates that decide whether the preferred-skills and education scores apply. The rubric contains no fairness instruction (e.g., “ignore name, gender, age”), allowing model behavior to be evaluated without such guidance. For a scored question q∈Qq\in Q with levels 0,…,ℓq0,\dots,\ell_{q}, the normalized criterion score aq∈[0,1]a_{q}\in[0,1] is

aq={1ℓq​∑v=0ℓqv​pq​(v)for Decision Models,v^qℓqfor Generative Models,\displaystyle a_{q}=\begin{cases}\frac{1}{\ell_{q}}\sum_{v=0}^{\ell_{q}}v\,p_{q}(v)&\text{for Decision Models{}},\\[4.0pt] \frac{\hat{v}_{q}}{\ell_{q}}&\text{for Generative Models{}},\end{cases}

where pq​(v)p_{q}(v) is the probability a Decision Model assigns to level vv and v^q\hat{v}_{q} is the level a Generative Model chooses. Preferred attributes count only if the model’s probability for their gate is at least 0.50.5 (gq=1g_{q}=1); otherwise gq=0g_{q}=0, and gq=1g_{q}=1 for all other questions. The match score sj​is_{ji} is the weighted mean of the counted criterion scores:

sj​i=100⋅∑q∈Qwq​gq​aq∑q∈Qwq​gq,\displaystyle s_{ji}=100\cdot\frac{\sum_{q\in Q}w_{q}\,g_{q}\,a_{q}}{\sum_{q\in Q}w_{q}\,g_{q}},

with weights wqw_{q} of 3030 (required skills), 2525 (relevant experience), 1515 (seniority), 1010 (domain), 1010 (preferred skills), 55 (education) and 55 (evidence). For label flips on hiring-fairness, the label function is λ⁡(sj​i)=Fit\lambda(s_{ji})=\textsc{Fit} if sj​i≥50s_{ji}\geq 50 and NotFit otherwise, with ℒ={Fit,NotFit}\mathcal{L}=\{\textsc{Fit},\textsc{NotFit}\}. On JD-Fit, a pair is predicted Fit if sj​i≥τs_{ji}\geq\tau, where τ\tau is chosen per model on the tuning set to maximize balanced accuracy.

Appendix C Prompts

An example of the prompt structure is provided in Figure 4. The prompt consists of system instructions and user-provided content. The latter includes the job description, the candidate’s CV, and the rubric questions.

For both hiring-fairness and JD-Fit, all models receive the same job description and CV, ensuring consistency in the information provided across models. The rubric questions reported in Table 7 are then presented differently depending on the model type. Decision Models receive the questions as structured, typed inputs (e.g., yes/no questions) and return a probability distribution over the available answer levels for each question in a single call. In contrast, Generative Models receive the rubric questions as part of the textual prompt, together with the system instructions, and return their answers in a predefined JSON format. This output contains a probability for each question and a selected answer level for each scored question.

Appendix D Implementation Details

Four models are evaluated, each receiving identical inputs across all datasets. The two Decision Models are JEV 1.13.0 TypeSafe AI (2026), which returns a probability for every answer and provides no sampling or seed options; and Laya44 4 convaiinnovations/laya-multilingual on Hugging Face., which is run locally on a single NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4060 GPU (8 GB) with max_len=8192. The two Generative Models are GPT-6 Luna and GPT-6.1 Sol, both accessed through the OpenAI Responses API using a strict JSON output schema, with temperature and reasoning effort left at their default settings. The API provides neither a seed nor, for these reasoning models, token log-probabilities. Table 8 reports the API cost for each model.

Appendix E Statistical Tests

All comparisons follow a paired design to control for differences between CVs, job descriptions, and experimental scenarios. For hiring-fairness, each effect is calculated as the difference between two versions of the same CV, evaluated against the same job description and differing only in the demographic information being tested. For implicit signals, results are first averaged across the names representing each group. Individual differences are then averaged across the 572 CVs to obtain the overall effect. Uncertainty is assessed using 95% percentile bootstrap confidence intervals (Efron and Tibshirani, 1993), based on 2,000 resamples. CVs are resampled for hiring-fairness, while job descriptions are resampled for JD-Fit to account for the dependence between CVs evaluated against the same job description (Field and Welsh, 2007). Two-sided p-values are calculated from the same resamples (Davison and Hinkley, 1997). An effect is considered statistically significant when its confidence interval excludes zero. For demographic analyses, multiple-testing corrections are applied separately for each model using the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure (Benjamini and Hochberg, 1995), with adjusted p-values below 0.05 indicating significance. For JD-Fit validity, AUC, balanced accuracy, and Precision@5 are evaluated against their respective chance-level benchmarks. Differences in AUC between models (Δ​AUC\Delta\mathrm{AUC}) are assessed using a paired bootstrap on the same resampled job descriptions, with significance determined by whether the confidence interval excludes zero.

Appendix F Sensitivity Analysis

On hiring-fairness, the threshold cut-off affects only the label-flip measure in Table 1, where a CV is labeled Fit if m≥50m\geq 50 and NoFit otherwise; all other measures use scores or ranks. The cut-off of 50 is the midpoint of the scale and is not calibrated. To test whether this article’s conclusions depend on it, label flips are recomputed from the scores of the same 7 runs at every integer cut-off from 5 to 95. At 50, this reproduces the values in Table 1.

Figure 5 shows that the ranking of the models is robust. GPT-6 Luna has the highest label-flip rate at all 91 cut-offs, peaking at 6.0%6.0\%. JEV has the lowest rate among the API models at every cut-off from 22 to 73. Outside this range, few CVs score near the cut-off, and JEV and GPT-6.1 Sol both flip at most 1.0% of labels. Instead, GPT-6.1 Sol matches or undercuts JEV at 23 of these cut-offs. Laya is deterministic and flips no labels at any cut-off. Rates peak where scores are dense, since a label changes only when run-to-run variation moves a score across the cut-off.
